issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes hypervigilance, startle, danger in silence, fragmented/avoided trauma memory, and appraisals of betrayal and injustice after police violence. Those other items describe a fearful, threat-sensitive presentation; endorsing active risk-taking as a core threat item pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported elsewhere in the selected nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself
issues.explanation: 'Can't Rely on Self' is a weaker fit than the other appraisals for this trauma/context. The profile is organized around external betrayal/injustice linked to police violence, but this item shifts to global self-distrust without corresponding self-blame, shame, incompetence, or strategy items elsewhere. In combination with the strong betrayal/injustice theme, it creates a less coherent appraisal profile.

vignette:
Carlos Mendez was a 54-year-old Latin American man who had spent most of his adult life in public service, and he came to treatment after months in which even ordinary workdays had begun to feel precarious. As a parole officer, he moved through offices, county buildings, parking lots, and neighborhood visits with the same steady routine he had managed for years, but after the traumatic incident he described, that routine no longer felt predictable to him. He said the event began when he was responding to a situation involving police violence, and what he remembered most was not only the force of it but the sense that the people and institutions around him, the ones he had trusted to keep things from becoming worse, had failed him completely. When he spoke about it, he often stopped before the account felt complete, as if he were pushing the memory away before he could fully enter it. Parts of what happened were vivid to him in fragments—the setting, certain voices, the shock of realizing what was unfolding—but he described the larger scene as strangely hard to hold together, “like it should belong to somebody else,” he said, because the memory felt so extreme that it was difficult for him to believe it had actually happened to him.

In the weeks that followed, Carlos found himself living with an almost constant sense that danger could emerge without warning. He noticed that unusual silence made him tense immediately, as if the absence of ordinary sound meant something dangerous was about to happen. At work, when a hallway went quiet or a waiting room went still, he became sharply aware of his own body and the space around him. He said he constantly scanned his surroundings for signs of danger, not in a dramatic or theatrical way, but in the practiced, exhausted manner of someone who felt he could not afford to miss anything. He watched hands, doors, posture, tone, and movement, and he startled easily at abrupt sounds or sudden motion. Even in the parking lot outside the parole office, he would pause before getting out of his car and look around longer than he used to, taking in the spaces between vehicles and the corners of the lot as if checking for something he could not quite name. At home, his wife noticed that he sat more rigidly at the table and reacted sharply to unexpected noises from the kitchen or television. He did not describe himself as panicked, but he spoke about being jumpy, as though his body remained prepared for trouble even during moments that should have been ordinary.

Certain sensations brought the event back with a force he found hard to tolerate. When his heart started racing or pounding, he immediately felt pulled toward the same sense of imminent danger he had felt during the incident, and that made him more careful about exertion, stress, and any moment that seemed to raise his pulse. He said stress itself had become a marked trigger; on days when the office was busy, when a supervisee behaved badly, or when a conversation became tense, he could feel himself tightening before the situation had even fully developed. What affected him deeply was not only the memory of the violence but the moral violation of it. He had always seen himself as someone who believed in rules, accountability, and restraint, so when he encountered people misbehaving now—disrespecting boundaries, escalating conflict, ignoring basic expectations—he felt a surge of disgust and alarm that was larger than the situation at hand. It was not that he became reckless or uncontrolled; rather, these moments seemed to confirm for him how quickly things could become unsafe when people failed to act responsibly. He had come to believe that what happened to him was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it, and that sense of injustice stayed with him in a quiet but persistent way. He also spoke of betrayal, saying plainly that he had been betrayed by someone he trusted. He did not elaborate in a dramatic fashion, but the statement carried real weight: he experienced the incident as proof that even those in positions meant to protect him could let him down, and that the institutions surrounding the event had not protected him when it mattered most.

Over time, Carlos changed the way he moved through both work and home life. He remained employed, but he described doing so with more vigilance and less ease. He was less willing to linger in situations that felt unpredictable, and he paid close attention to the sound level of a room, the emotional temperature of a conversation, and the way people around him were behaving. He did not want to be caught off guard again, and that determination shaped how he handled his daily environment. Eventually, the strain of maintaining that level of alertness, along with the continuing sense of unfairness and betrayal, brought him to seek help. What finally pushed him to come in was the feeling that he was no longer able to keep carrying the memory in fragments while still functioning as he wanted to at work and at home. He hoped to find some way to live with what had happened without feeling, every day, that another moment of silence, another racing heartbeat, or another misstep by someone else might mean danger was already close at hand.
